title_eng: Adaptive motion artifacts reduction algorithm for ECG signal in textile wearable sensor
abstract:
For ubiquitous healthcare system, it is very important to
measure a bio-signal without any discomfort. The electro-conductive
fabric can be a good application for biomedical sensor. However, it
is diﬃcult to measure the bio-signal because of its sensitivity varia-
tion caused by contact impedance change, especially by motion of the
subject. In this paper, adaptive noise reduction algorithm on motion
artifacts is described to measure electro-cardiogram using lead II con-
ﬁguration conducted with both Ag/AgCl electrode as a reference signal
and electro-conductive fabric.

1 Introduction
Nowadays, ubiquitous environment is a popular topic among researchers.
Digital convergence enables people to connect to any device with ease, any-
where and anytime. Particularly, in bio-medical engineering, new trend using
‘e’ of electronic and ‘u’ of ubiquitous, called e-Health or u-Health is emerging.
Novel systems and applications using information and communication tech-
nology (ICT) are required to measure bio-signals without any discomforts or
time-space limitation.
Researchers are interested in wearable devices for ubiquitous healthcare
environment on the ground of its portability, ﬂexibility and connectivity [1].
This type of sensor has an advantage for the patient who is in rehabilitation
therapy, or for a person who needs all-day nursing, to monitor one’s health
status with relatively less cost and without any or little limitation in space
and time [2].
In this point of approach, wearable sensor with electro-conductive fabric
has comfortable texture and is easy to use because it is a wearing type rather
than the existing bio-signal sensor of the adhesive type conventional ECG
electrode [3]. However, the sensor also has some issues that it is weak to AC
power line interference (e.g. 50/60 Hz), thermal noise and motion artifacts,
because of very low impedance characteristic.
Among theses weaknesses, motion artifacts caused by the subject’s move-
ment have such various frequency ranges that their reduction is harder than
the others which have speciﬁc frequency ranges. In addition, its magnitude
is relatively large that meaningful bio-signals can be buried in it. This can
lead to a wrong diagnosis result and improper follow-up [4].
There are several researches on reducing motion artifacts by considering it
as a simple sinusoidal noise in conventional ECG electrode. Gary M. Friesen,
et al. [5] compared noise sensitivity in detecting QRS mentioning that motion
of ECG electrode caused electrode-skin impedance changes inducing baseline
changes with its duration of 100 ∼ 500 ms. Antti Ruha, et al . [6] proposed
real-time QRS detector system for measuring ambulatory HRV. The motion
artifacts were considered to be lower than 5 Hz sinusoidal wave and ﬁltered

Some researchers are interested in motion artifacts as a more complicated
noise source. D. A. Tong, et al . [4] proposed adaptive ﬁlter for electrode
motion artifact caused by relation between the subject’s skin and electrode.
Yan Liu and Michael G. Pecht [7] also proposed adaptive ﬁltering for motion
artifacts considered as a skin stretch using LED and optical sensor.
In spite of more complex situation than the conventional electrode men-
tioned above, there are few considerations on motion artifacts, so far, in ECG
signal acquired by means of electro-conductive fabrics. To reduce the motion
artifacts for ECG measured by electro-conductive textile wearable sensor,
we suggest adaptive ﬁlter method using motion artifacts model in 2 motion
types and its quantitative evaluation using statistical analysis.
2 Mathematical background
2.1 Adaptive ﬁlter system
Fig. 1 (a) shows the system block diagram of adaptive ﬁlter. Let x(n) be
the signal input consisting of the original ECG signal source v(n) and the
unknown motion artifacts noise source m(n) added by a subject. Let the
desired input r(n) be correlated with m(n) but not correlated with v(n).
The y(n) is the adaptive ﬁlter output. Suppose that v, r and m have zero
mean in stationary random properties.
The system output e(n) can be formulated as follows:
e(n) = x(n) − y(n)
= v(n) + m(n) − y(n) (1)
Squaring followed by mean of Eq. (1) is
E{e(n)2} = E{v(n)2} + E{(m(n) − y(n))2} (2)
The right-hand side term of Eq. (2) must be minimized for minimizing
E{e(n)2}, so optimal solution is
y(n) = m(n) (3)
That is, when the desired motion input r(n) is chosen to high correlation
with m(n), if we ﬁnd y(n) by r(n) then the system output e(n) will be close
to the original ECG signal source v(n) with its motion artifacts reduced.

3 Methods
3.1 Speciﬁcation of sensors
A round-type conventional Ag/AgCl electrode (generally, 2 kΩ @ 10 Hz) and
the electro-conductive fabric (conductive coated on polyester, 3 cm × 3c m ,
0.15 ∼ 0.20 Ω/sq.inch) are used for the experiment. Its appearance and mi-
croscopic image are in Fig. 2 (a)–(b).
3.2 System conﬁguration
Lead II conﬁguration is conducted with both sensors, and ECGs are acquired
by BIOPACr© MP 150 with ECG ampliﬁer module (ECG100C, set its gain
to 1,000 times) simultaneously. This conﬁguration is illustrated in Fig. 2 (c).
The sampling frequency is 1,000 Hz, higher than general cases (250∼ 500 Hz)
in ECG acquisition. This is for other feature extraction and future study
like [6], such as QRS detection or HRV calculation in better time-resolution
condition.
3.3 Activity control
In the experiment, subject movement is restricted to 2 types:
1. Sitting down a chair and standing (small z-axis movement, every 10
seconds)
2. Squatting and standing (big z-axis movement, every 4 seconds)
